source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic: limitations of mathematical reasoning (GSM-NoOp section)
finding: Adding one inconsequential clause (No-Op) to grade-school problems cut accuracy for every model, including o1-preview and o1-mini. Showing 8 shots of the same question with the same kind of clause did not fix it.
numbers: 8-shot, GSM-Symbolic vs Symbolic-NoOp: GPT-4o 94.9 -> 63.1; GPT-4o-mini 91.7 -> 54.1; Phi-3-medium 82.5 -> 29.4; Gemma2-9b-it 79.1 -> 22.3. Fig 8a drops: o1-preview -17.5 points, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o-mini -40.0; Phi-3-mini over 65%.
quote: models tend to convert statements to operations without truly understanding their meaning
limits: Clauses are 'seemingly relevant'; the dataset was never released, so the drop cannot be split into lost rule vs reasonable use of the clause (see d03). o1 models are 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: even a 2024 reasoning model drops 17.5 points on a one-clause twin. Our twin test must audit the distractor first.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic appendix A.5 and Fig 13 (o1 failure case)
finding: o1-preview is robust across difficulty levels of GSM-Symbolic but still falls on NoOp. A shown failure: it applied a 10% inflation that the problem said was irrelevant because prices were for this year.
numbers: No exact o1 NoOp accuracy in the text; only the Fig 8a drops quoted in d01.
limits: Error signature is a named one: a number or phrase is turned into an operation (discount -> multiply, inflation -> multiply, smaller fruit -> subtract).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a code check can count 'operation applied for an irrelevant quantity' by comparing the program the model writes against the gold program (does the program use the distractor value?).

source: Sturb (2026, 5 June) Revisiting GSM-Symbolic: models seem to reason okay, actually (LessWrong post, not peer reviewed)
finding: A 2026 re-run with GPT-4o, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5. Unaudited distractors reproduce the original drop. After two LLM auditors keep only truly irrelevant clauses, the drop is 0-2 points and not different from zero.
numbers: 1,000 GSM-Symbolic questions per model (100 templates x 10). 945 usable generated distractors; 117 (12.4%) passed the audit. Auditors Claude Opus and GPT-5.5 agreed at kappa 0.32; they kept 12% and 36%. 8-shot CoT. Exact per-model values only in charts.
limits: Distractors written by Opus 4.6, not Apple's hand-written ones; audit by LLMs with low agreement; effort settings not stated; single author; only 3 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 4: most of the NoOp drop may be ambiguous distractors, not a lost rule. Only 12% of generated distractors were clean, so twin sets need a human or two-auditor check.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025, COLM) Cats confuse reasoning LLM: query-agnostic adversarial triggers (CatAttack)
finding: A short irrelevant suffix (for example 'cats sleep most of their lives') found on a cheap proxy transfers to reasoning models and raises their error rate. Absolute rates are small.
numbers: 225 problems from 9 NuminaMath sources, 6 runs. DeepSeek R1 combined attack success 4.50% vs 1.50% random (3x); R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00% (2.83x). Proxy DeepSeek V3 success 35%; transfer to R1 about 20% (114 prompts). Authors report up to +500% error for reasoning models and +700% for instruction models on 1,000 GSM8K problems.
limits: Triggers were selected adversarially against a proxy, so rates are worst-case, not typical. Absolute error stays low (a few percent).
agent_relevance: Gap 2: 2025 reasoning models (R1, QwQ, Qwen3, Phi-4-reasoning, o1, o3-mini) still move on irrelevant text, by a small absolute amount. Test the scaffold with a fixed suffix set.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) CatAttack semantic filtering and slowdown (sections 2.4, 3)
finding: Two human checks on the successful R1 attacks: only part of them kept the original meaning, and most of those were true failures. Triggers also made reasoning longer.
numbers: 3 blinded annotators solved each pair; 60% of modified problems judged consistent with the original (unanimity). About 80% of those showed a true wrong answer. Slowdown (response at least 1.5x / 2x / 4x length): o1 26.4/9.9/1.3%; o3-mini 16.8/6.0/3.0%; R1 28.0/16.2/4.8%; R1-distill-Qwen-32B 42.17/32.5/15.33%.
limits: Slowdown tables cover 225-problem and GSM8K runs; judge model sensitivity checked with Gemini 2.5 Flash only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: 40% of automatically generated 'same-meaning' twins were not the same problem. Count a twin only after a consistency check. Equal-token control matters because triggers cost tokens.

source: Li et al. (2024) GSM-Plus: robustness of LLMs as math problem solvers (Table 4)
finding: Eight perturbation types of GSM8K (numeric, arithmetic, distractor insertion, critical thinking and others). Accuracy falls for all 25 models; the strongest model falls least.
numbers: GPT-4: GSM8K 93.25 -> GSM-Plus 85.58, performance drop rate 8.23%, ASP 81.54. GPT-3.5-Turbo: 73.62 -> 61.19, PDR 16.88%, ASP 51.36. Math-SFT does not cut PDR: MetaMath-Mistral-7B 33.86%.
limits: 2024 models; PDR = 1 - accuracy on twins / accuracy on seeds. ASP is the share of pairs where seed and twin are both right.
agent_relevance: A paired seed-twin design with PDR and ASP is a ready metric for our twin test.

source: Li et al. (2024) GSM-Plus Table 5: prompting methods on the twin set
finding: The closest source to gap 1. Prompting scaffolds were run on seeds and on twins with GPT-3.5-Turbo. Gains held in absolute terms on the twins but the seed-twin gap stayed the same size. A compositional method helped the 'critical thinking' twins most.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GSM8K / GSM-Plus / critical-thinking subset: CoT 74.17 / 62.92 / 40.83; Least-to-most 74.17 / 62.60 / 39.17; Compositional (COMP) 76.67 / 65.52 / 54.17; CoT+SC (5 samples) 76.67 / 66.88 / 40.00; COMP+SC 80.00 / 69.47 / 55.83. Gap seeds vs twins: CoT 11.25, COMP+SC 10.53.
quote: it does not bridge the performance gap of LLMs between the standard benchmark and the adversarial benchmark
limits: Not equal tokens: SC uses 5 samples and COMP uses iterative calls. One model, grade-school math. Authors: it 'does not bridge the performance gap'.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (partly closed, one model): a scaffold gain carried to the twins but did not shrink the gap. Our test should report gain on twin, gap, and tokens.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: Scaffolds help on distractor twins: self-consistency and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction both add accuracy, but most base problems still fail on at least one distractor variant.
numbers: code-davinci-002, micro / macro accuracy on GSM-IC-4K: CoT 72.4 / 6.0; CoT+instruction 77.8 / 15.0; LTM 77.5 / 18.0; LTM+instruction 80.6 / 25.0; CoT+SC (20 samples) 88.1 / 30.0; LTM+SC 93.4 / 45.0. Correct answer present in 20 samples for 99.7% of problems. Macro = base problem solved under all distractor variants.
limits: 2023 model; the instruction adds about 5 points; best macro 45% means over half of base problems are still hit. Table text was extracted from a two-column layout and read by position.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 4: use macro accuracy (all twins of one seed solved), not only mean accuracy. The correct answer is often in the sample set, so a verify-then-pick step can use it.

source: Zhao et al. (2026 v6) Is chain-of-thought reasoning of LLMs a mirage? A data distribution lens (DataAlchemy)
finding: Models trained from scratch on a clean synthetic world give full CoT accuracy in distribution and near zero when the task, length or format shifts. The reasoning text stays fluent but the answer is wrong.
numbers: Task-shift table: ID exact match 100.00%; partly out-of-distribution (POOD) 0.00%; fully OOD 0.00%; edit distance 0 / 0.1671 / 0.2997; BLEU 1 / 0.4538 / 0.2947.
limits: Small models trained from scratch, abstract letter transformations, not a frontier model or a scaffold; no equal-token control.
agent_relevance: Gap 1, 4: a fluent chain is not proof of a held rule. A lost rule has a signature: ID perfect, shifted zero, with no partial credit.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024/2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs (extended version)
finding: Extended counterfactual study: letter-string analogies with altered alphabets, digit matrices and story analogies. Humans stay high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply on simple altered-alphabet problems. Story analogies show answer-order and paraphrase sensitivity.
numbers: Tested GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and human samples; confidence intervals are binomial 95%. Exact table values were not re-read this session; the earlier row values (human 0.753, GPT-3 0.488 and so on) are in claims K08 sources b17.
limits: Only GPT-3/3.5/4 era. No 2025-2026 reasoning model appears. Drop is smaller on harder (multi-generalisation) problems because both groups do poorly.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for altered alphabets: no 2025-2026 reasoning-model run was found.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: When an instruction arrives in pieces, models answer early on guessed assumptions and then stick to that first answer. The loss is mostly unreliability, not aptitude. Reasoning models o3 and R1 fail the same way.
numbers: 15 LLMs, over 200,000 simulated conversations, 6 generation tasks. Average drop 39% (top models about -35%); aptitude -15% but unreliability +112%. Lowering temperature to 0 did not restore reliability. Recap and snowball turns recovered only part.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Underspecified instructions, not a salient wrong move on a fixed task. Simulated users.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: closest LLM analogue to failing to inhibit a salient early answer. It is a premature commit that is not undone. A code gate that blocks the final answer until all fields are filled is testable.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot
finding: The same injected error is fixed when it is attributed to the user and missed when attributed to the model itself. Appending the word 'Wait' after the model's own error cuts the gap sharply.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: blind spot 64.5% on average (62.8% on logic and object tracking); 41.4% for Sonnet 4 and 52.5% for Haiku. Share of a model's own natural errors caught when shown externally: 4.3-10.8%. 'Wait' lowers the blind spot 89.3% and raises mean accuracy 156%; fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces lowers it 76.0%. Correction markers 179.5% more frequent for external errors on GSM8K-SC.
limits: Injected errors, not natural retry loops; mostly open non-reasoning models; GPT-5.4 used as a judge with 95.0% three-way agreement.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 9: a cheap gate works. A forced 'Wait'-style recheck step after the first answer is a clean inhibition fix to test, scored on identical errors labelled own vs other.

source: Lam et al. (2025) CodeCrash: exposing LLM fragility to misleading natural language in code reasoning
finding: Perturbed code tasks give a countable error signature: the model follows a misleading comment or print message instead of what the code does. Reasoning models are more robust but a plausible wrong hint can send them into long self-checking.
numbers: 1,279 questions (CRUXEval, LiveCodeBench), 17 LLMs plus o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B. Output prediction, direct: average -23.2%; with CoT: -13.8%. Reasoning models: negligible loss under structure changes, but a plausible wrong hint (MHC) gives 2-3x tokens; QwQ-32B had 4 'collapse' events (20k tokens then 12k 'Hmm'); for o3-mini more effort made the drop worse.
limits: Per-model reasoning-model table rows were garbled in text extraction, so figures are not assigned to single models. 17 models are 2024-early 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the signature 'answer matches the planted comment, not the executed result' can be counted by running the code. Report hint-adoption rate next to accuracy.

source: Samiei et al. (2026, CogSci) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Adults do well on conjunctive rules when they choose their own tests. LLMs were tested only in the active setting, so the paper gives no passive-vs-active LLM contrast at equal tokens.
numbers: 6 models (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, o4-mini, deepseek-chat), 24 trials per rule type, 48 per model, 288 trials, temperature 0. Hypothesis space 32. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner near-perfect on disjunctive; on conjunctive, strong models stay below top humans, deepseek-chat and o4-mini only modestly above baseline. Humans: 16% wrong on rule and objects, 16% right rule wrong objects; model errors are often one wrong object.
limits: Intro says LLMs 'do not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions' but no LLM passive arm is described in the methods read. Exact per-model accuracies are in figures. Tokens not matched.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: no study found with an LLM run-a-test-first arm vs a no-test arm at equal tokens on conjunctive rules.

source: Seed, Tebbich, Emery, Clayton (2006) Investigating physical cognition in rooks, Corvus frugilegus. Curr Biol 16:697-701 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Independent lab, non-tool-using corvid, two-trap tube task. Almost all rooks solved the first task and passed a change of stimuli, but only one passed the two transfer tasks with no shared visual constant.
numbers: 7 of 8 rooks solved the initial task; all 7 transferred across a change of stimuli; 6 of 7 failed the two further transfer tasks; 1 female solved them.
limits: Abstract only. Rooks, not crows; no tool use needed. This is the design that Taylor 2009 copied.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 (partly closed): the same shape of result (solve, then fail a transfer that removes visual constants) appears in another lab and another corvid.

source: Tebbich, Seed, Emery, Clayton (2007) Non-tool-using rooks solve the trap-tube problem. Anim Cogn 10:225-231 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: A second rook study with a modified tube. Some birds solve it. None pass the novel transfer tasks.
numbers: 3 of 7 rooks solved the modified trap-tube; 0 passed the novel transfer tasks.
limits: Abstract only. Same lab group as d15.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: independent of Taylor's lab (same group as d15, different from the crow lab). Pass then fail-transfer, again.

source: Tebbich et al. (2012) Physical cognition and tool-use: performance of Darwin's finches in the two-trap tube task. Anim Cogn (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Two finch species on the two-trap tube. Few solve; none of the solvers transfer when features change. Tool use did not predict success.
numbers: 0 small tree finches and 2 non-tool-using woodpecker finches solved the initial task; 1 tool-using woodpecker finch solved it with its own tool; none transferred.
limits: Abstract only; very small numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a non-corvid, different lab, same pattern.

source: Mulcahy and Call (2006) How great apes perform on a modified trap-tube task. Anim Cogn 9:193-199 (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Apes allowed to rake instead of push avoided the trap only when it was functional, but failed the original push version. Probe format decides the pass.
numbers: 5 orangutans, 2 chimpanzees, 2 bonobos, 1 gorilla; 2 orangutans and 1 chimpanzee avoided the functional trap in the rake task but failed the push task; all but one preferred to rake.
limits: Abstract only. Primates, 10 subjects.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 context. A pass in one interface and failure in another echoes Mecattaf's interface worry (gap 7).

source: [Solution of trap tube test by hooded crows (Corvus cornix L.)] (2013), Russian journal (abstract via Europe PMC; authors not shown in the record)
finding: A corvid study from a third group with a piston-in-a-tube design. Few birds solve the trap task by foresight; most by trial and error, and transfer used concrete rules.
numbers: 8 hooded crows; 6 learned the non-trap tube; 1 of those 6 passed the trap task on the first trial; 4 learned it by trial and error; 2 transfer tasks solved with 'rather concrete rules'.
limits: Abstract only; the URL is a search page. Not a two-hole copy of the New Caledonian task.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 (partly closed): a trap-tube follow-up with another crow species supports the shallow-rule reading. No Gray, Jelbert, Seed or Bird two-hole follow-up was found in search.

source: Hennefield, Hwang, Weston, Povinelli (2018) Meta-analytic techniques reveal that corvid causal reasoning in the Aesop's Fable paradigm is driven by trial-and-error learning. Anim Cogn
finding: Insertion-level analysis shows corvids improve after an efficient choice but not after an inefficient one, and learning does not carry across tasks.
numbers: 28 subjects (rooks, Eurasian jays, New Caledonian crows), 5 articles, insertions per subject 1-150, cut-off median 63. Water vs sand (N=22): after inefficient choice OR 0.67 [0.43, 1.05], p=.08; after efficient OR 5.00 [2.66, 9.38], p<.001; difference p<.001. Float vs sink (N=18): after inefficient OR 1.57 [0.55, 4.44]; after efficient OR 2.43 [1.23, 4.80], p=.01. Slope per insertion OR 1.04 and 1.05. Task order OR 0.81 [0.57, 1.14], p=.22 (all tasks); 1.43 [0.99, 2.08], p=.06 (successful tasks).
limits: Hollow vs solid task (N=11) showed no learning and was excluded. Paper gives inconsistent task counts (33 vs 16). Same work as a10 and b11.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 method: log the choice before and after each outcome and fit odds of repeating the efficient choice by previous outcome. This is the template for per-attempt LLM logs.

source: Mecattaf et al. (2024) A little less conversation, a little more action, please (LLMs in Animal-AI): per-level reporting and interface limits
finding: Exact per-level LLM accuracies are not in the text; they are bars in Figures 3 and 4 only. The text gives the shape. No paper citing it was found that swaps the image-and-action-script interface for a tool API.
numbers: Per level 12 trials (3 runs x 4 tasks); 59 children and top-10 competition agents as reference; LLMs capped at 30 action scripts per episode. LLMs pass some tasks in levels 1-2, sporadic in 5, 6, 8; comparable to competition agents in 3, 8, 9, 10 at very low rates; children better in all levels. In-context expert example: no notable change; GPT rose in levels 2 and 3, Gemini fell, Claude mixed.
limits: Authors write the control challenge may dominate the cognitive one and name frame-by-frame control and fine-tuning as future work. Semantic Scholar citing list (16 items) shows no tool-API rerun. Search for 2025-2026 follow-ups was limited by rate limits.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Do not quote per-level numbers; use the shape and the interface caveat.

source: Learning from others' mistakes? limits on understanding a trap-tube task by young chimpanzees and children (2007, J Comp Psychol 121:12; abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: Chimpanzees and young children saw a model's errors and successes. Seeing errors did not speed learning. Two of 6 chimpanzees built an anticipatory strategy without showing causal understanding; 3-4 year olds copied actions regardless of relevance.
numbers: 2-7 year old chimpanzees (6) and 3-4 year old children did not benefit from observing errors; 5-6 year olds mastered the task without benefit from errors.
limits: Abstract only. Observational learning, not own-attempt learning.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the human-and-ape version of 'errors teach little' agrees with Hennefield. Compare to LLM retry logs where the failed attempt is shown.
